# Cūḷamālukya Sutta (MN 63 (PTS MN i 426))

**ID:** MN 63 (PTS MN i 426)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷamālukya Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 426  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷamālukya Sutta* (MN 63; PTS MN i 426–432), also titled *Cūḷamālukyovāda Sutta*, is the sixty-third discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Catalog; Davis and Flanagan 2014; Le 2018]. In this discourse, the monk Mālunkyāputta (or Mālunkāputta) approaches the Buddha demanding a definitive declaration on ten speculative metaphysical questions—whether the world is eternal or not eternal, finite or infinite, whether the soul and body are identical or different, and whether a Tathāgata exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist after death—threatening to abandon the monastic life if these remain unexplained [Davis and Flanagan 2014; Galasek 2016]. The Buddha responds by pointing out that he never promised to explain these speculative matters, illustrating Mālunkyāputta's folly through the celebrated parable of a man pierced with a poisoned arrow who refuses the surgeon's help until he discovers the identity, caste, and physical characteristics of the archer, as well as the materials of the bow and arrow; such a man would die before obtaining answers to his irrelevant inquiries [Moult 2012; Davis and Flanagan 2014; Crosby 2014]. The Buddha states that these points are left undeclared (*avyākata*) because they are not beneficial, fundamental to the holy life, or conducive to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, calming, direct knowledge, and awakening [Foo Meng Jee 2013; Galasek 2016]. Scholars highlight the Buddha's pedagogical method of counter-questioning (*paṭipucchā*) deployed in the sutta to redirect the interlocutor toward liberation from suffering [Le 2018].

- [Davis and Flanagan 2014] Davis and Flanagan, A Mirror Is for Reflection: Understanding Buddhist Ethics — PTS page span (MN i 426–432), Mālunkyāputta's demands on speculative views, and the medical analogy.
- [Foo Meng Jee 2013] Foo Meng Jee, Modern Reflection on Buddhist Views of Cyclic Existence and Cosmology (2013) — Quotations on why the Buddha leaves cosmological and speculative questions undeclared.
- [Galasek 2016] Bruno Galasek, On Presenting Characters and Representation of Persons... Characters in Narrative Suttas of the Majjhima Nikaya (2016) — Listing and Pali text of the ten undeclared speculative views (MN i 426) and discussion of the arrow simile.
- [Le 2018] Ngoc Cuong Le, Text and Context: Hermeneutical Study of Ways the Buddha Answers Questions (2018) — Analysis of pedagogical counter-questioning (paṭipucchā) and purpose of the poison arrow discourse.
- [Crosby 2014] Kate Crosby, Theravada Buddhism: Continuity, Diversity, and Identity (2014) — Context on metaphysical speculation versus spiritual progress and the poisoned arrow parable.
